doc.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Playing live and covering mistakes
summary: Audience communication and older Chicago musicians' advice to play through mistakes loudly.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you about that and let you kind of expound on that for just a moment, and that would be when you play live, do you feel like there is an immediate need for communication to an audience first rather than a tape recorder? Or is there a communal degree of communication going back and forth between you and them?

I think it’s more of a communal thing going back and forth. The musician is spinning off of what the audience is giving him. You need that. Especially if you’ve got one that’s in your corner all the way, you need that. There’s nothing better than that. Actually I don’t think much about it before I’m playing as to how they’re going to react, I’m just happy that they’re there. And I figure if they’re there, they’re there to hear us. And we normally get a good response. And that’s what I feel about it. But when you’re in a studio, there’s nobody there but the producer, the engineer and a forest of microphones. Not much inspiration you can get off that except playing with the guys you know, with the rest of the group. But it’s not the same as playing live. And you’re going to make mistakes, but that’s jazz. But the thing of it is, a good jazz musician, you know, in fact it’s one of the things I learned from the older guys in Chicago, well to put it bluntly, one guy told me he says, “When you make a mistake,” he says “forget about it. Play right through it.” He says, “Just say to yourself oops, and keep going. And nobody will know it’s a mistake but you.” He said, “When you make a mistake, make it loud and wrong. Don’t make it soft. That way it stands out like a mistake. But if you just make it loud — ‘oh, look what he did there, oh, yeah, I got to listen to that again.’ After that everybody else will be doing it.” Like with Charlie Parker’s “Lover Man.”
Or one person said, we were talking, I was playing with a band and we were talking about that same thing and he said, “If you make a mistake, play the same thing a third lower. Sequence it.”
Yeah. I never thought about that, yeah.
Now we’re going to hear you do that.
That’s the joy in playing jazz. You’re going to make a mistake and then you can turn a negative thing into a positive thing. And I think this is what makes it fun.
